title: Pauri 5, meaning: one Giver
hookLine: He cannot be installed or made; the Guru has given one understanding, that there is one Giver of all, never to be forgotten (Japji 5)

lines: THE GIFT BECOMES PART OF YOU.
cards: Have you ever forgotten who gave you something? A sweater you've worn for years, and one day you realize you have no idea where it came from. A habit picked up from a teacher whose name is gone.
People forget givers all the time, not out of ingratitude, just because the gift becomes part of them. The fifth pauri ends with Nanak asking for one thing only: not to forget the Giver.

teach.b: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. He cannot be installed or made; He is Himself, by Himself, the stainless one. Those who serve Him receive honor.
Nanak, sing of the treasure of virtues.
Sing, listen, and keep love in your heart: pain will leave, and peace will come home. Then a run of lines about the Guru's word.
Through the Guru comes the sound, through the Guru the scripture, and through the Guru the One is everywhere. The Guru, it says, is Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma; the Guru is Parvati, the mother.
Sikh commentators read this as saying that everything people honor in those great names is found in the Guru's word.
Then Nanak says something disarmingly honest: even if I knew Him, I couldn't describe Him; there's no telling it. And then the refrain. Guraa ik dehi bujhaaee: O Guru, give me this one understanding.
Sabhnaa jeeaa kaa ik daataa, so mai visar na jaaee: of all living beings there is one Giver; may I not forget Him.
Visar is to forget, to let slip from the mind; na jaaee, may it not happen. That's the whole request.
Not wealth, not answers to every question, not even the power to describe God. Just memory. If there is one Giver of everything, forgetting the Giver is the main thing that can go wrong.
And remembering is simran, the practice from camp three, the thing Japji's title word, jap, asks for.

how: Sikhs recite the fifth pauri each morning; its refrain, that there is one Giver of all beings who should never be forgotten, is also sung as kirtan.

o: to give away, to share freely
to forget, to let slip from mind
to give thanks for what you have

games.q: what's inside the pauri — tap the pairs.
p: O Guru, give me one understanding

s: Nanak asks the Guru for wealth
he asks for one understanding: there is one Giver, may I not forget Him.
the pauri says Nanak could describe God if he knew Him
even knowing Him, he says, there's no telling it.
the refrain names one Giver of all living beings

games.q: Nanak could ask the Guru for anything. what's the one understanding he asks for?
o: that there's one Giver of all, and may he not forget Him.
the right words to describe God.
games.why: sabhnaa jeeaa kaa ik daataa, so mai visar na jaaee: one Giver of all; may I not forget Him.

practice: Choose one thing within reach, something you're wearing or the cup you last drank from, and trace it back: who made it, grew it, carried it, paid for it, until the chain runs out into rain and soil and sun.
Notice how many hands there are, and where they all begin. If you pray, you can thank the one Giver with a single word, Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Visar. To forget, to let slip from the mind: the one thing Nanak asks never to do, of the one Giver of all beings.
